Summary
DeepInfer currently runs on SM100 and Ascend 950. This PR adds an SM90 (Hopper) path so that DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash runs end to end on Hopper GPUs, validated on 8x and 4x NVIDIA H20-3e (141 GB):
same checkpoint, no conversion
attention DP / CP, MoE EP, DSpark
CUDA graphs on
Key design points:
The MXFP4 routed experts stay resident in FP4, so 4 GPUs are enough.
FlashMLA's last Hopper kernels (
ba89a34
) are extended to the V4.1 KV cache formats.
SM100 and Ascend behaviour is unchanged. Every SM90 path is selected by
PLATFORM.is_sm90
, and all new kernels live in
deepinfer/model_executor/layers/sm90_ops/
.

Overview
This is the DSpark half of the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash specialized decode on GB300 (
#61868
). With
decode_backend
set to
latency_specialized
, it:
gives the DSpark draft model a decode executor of its own, on the target executor's kernels and streams;
fuses the Markov sampling loop, and shards it by vocabulary over the TP ranks at small batches;
captures the work between the target forward and the draft forward (sampling, the request-state update and the draft input preparation) in a CUDA graph.
With the switch off, the only shared change is that DFlash-family drafters prepare all their KV-cache groups in one launch, with the same outputs.
Depends on
#61868
and is stacked on it. Until that lands, this branch also contains its commits; only the last commit, the DSpark changes, is under review here.
Claims
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on one GB300 tray with DSpark, the switch on in both arms, this PR against
#61868
:
Decode step:
another 6.4% faster at batch 1
(4,354 → 4,075 µs), 4.3% at batch 8 and 1.9% at batch 32. Together with
[Perf][DSv4.1] DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash specialized decode on GB300
#61868
, the batch-1 step is about 24% faster than with the switch off.
InferenceX AgentX traces: P90 interactivity up another 5–10% at concurrency 1 to 32. At concurrency 64, turns finish sooner, so the closed loop admits more requests: throughput per GPU rises 15% and TTFT p50 falls from 5.55 to 1.46 s, while P90 interactivity drops 12% at the larger batch.
Accuracy and the DSpark acceptance length are unchanged.

Design notes
Structure.
The DSpark draft model registers itself when it is built with the switch on. The target's model state from
#61868
then builds the draft's executor right after the target's, on the same fused kernel, mailbox and mHC side stream, and the draft model's forward asks it for a step the same way (
plan()

run()

post_forward_cudagraphs

vllm/v1/worker/gpu/post_forward_cudagraph.py

With the switch off.
The only shared change is the multi-group prepare:
Group 0 writes the shared outputs, and each group writes its own query and context slot mappings.
prepare_context_anchor
now runs after the input preparation. LiLiCorr's anchor reads only target hidden states and
query_start_loc
, which that kernel does not write.
The padding loops use a fixed 1,024-wide block.
With the switch off, no model state offers post-forward graphs, so
PostForwardCudaGraphs.create
returns None, and the DSpark model shares no Markov weights, so the eager loop is unchanged.
Post-forward graphs: correctness and limits.
Eligibility.
Uniform decode steps without logprobs, prompt logprobs, grammar or logits processing. It is decided per step on the host, from state every TP rank holds identically.
Sampling draws.
They come from per-request seeds and positions, so a replay draws what the eager kernels draw.
Step tensors.
The per-step tensors that
prepare_inputs
allocates are copied into buffers the graphs own, in one launch. So are the host-backed temperature, seed and prefill-length buffers, which rotate through a small pool of pinned host buffers; the region reads the copies.
Graph key.
It holds the addresses of the other inputs, so a moved buffer captures a new graph instead of replaying a stale one. A batch shape therefore has one key.
Replay.
A replay waits for the previous step's output copy stream.
Capture and memory.
The first step of a shape runs eagerly, and the second captures. Graphs are captured while serving, into one memory pool of their own that the start-up memory profile does not see. That pool holds about one region's temporaries at the largest batch, mostly its logits.
Limit.
Past 32 graphs, further shapes run eagerly, which costs performance only.
Trade-off.
On graph steps, the async copy of the sampled tokens starts after the draft input preparation instead of before
postprocess_sampled
.
Sharded chain: rank lockstep.
The exchange is a cross-rank spin inside the draft step and its FULL graph, so every rank must launch it the same number of times.
Installation depends only on configuration, and CPU MIN all-reduces at load make the ranks agree on it.
The per-call choice depends only on the padded batch shape. It applies up to 8 request rows (4 at 8 ranks).
Steady state reads nothing back from the GPU.
The draws reproduce the fused path, except for the bias reduction order before its BF16 rounding, so a bias element can differ from cuBLAS's in its last bit.

#59511

Details
Kernel.
The MMA runs swapped: 64 experts form the wgmma M dimension and tokens the N dimension (32 to 128 per CTA), so small batches still fill the instruction. One TMA warp brings fp32 weight tiles and bf16 token tiles into shared memory. The MMA warpgroup reads each k16 slice of its weight fragment as fp32 and splits it in registers into three bf16 terms. Each term keeps the top 16 bits of what is left, so the three terms sum back to the weight bit for bit. It then issues register-A wgmma against the token tile, and splits the next slice while the current one runs. Products with bf16 activations are exact in fp32, so all error comes from accumulation:
The first-term products go to a tensor-core partial that starts from zero every K-tile (64 or 128 wide). It is then added into an fp32 register accumulator.
The second and third terms are about 2^-8 of the output. They keep their own partial across K, as the SM100 kernel does. This is the one numerical change from the Triton revision, which promoted all three terms every K-tile. It makes the largest tiles up to 9% faster. The worst MAE in my checks is 0.87x of the fp32 SGEMM's (GLM-4.7 shape, 7 tokens).
Split-K uses a thread-block cluster of up to 8 CTAs. Each CTA writes its partial tile to its own shared memory, reusing the weight stages, and after a cluster barrier sums one slice of the tile over all peers through DSMEM, in rank order. Results are deterministic, and there is no workspace and no second kernel. There is no host sync and no data-dependent shape, so the op is safe to capture in CUDA graphs.

There is no autotuning.

scores 4 tiles x 4 splits with a fixed cost model: waves times per-CTA time. A wave is one CTA per SM, and clusters of 4 or 8 only fill 15/16 of the SMs (120 of 132; at one CTA per SM,

gives 30 clusters of 4 and 15 of 8 on H200). The per-tile costs were fitted to H200 timings.
